blocks.text: The reality of email triage for executive assistants

When you ask how do executive assistants manage emails, the answer is rarely about speed. It is about discernment. An inbox is a list of tasks written by other people. If you treat it like a queue to be cleared, you will burn out. High-performing assistants treat the inbox as a firewall. Your goal is to stop noise from reaching the executive while ensuring that critical requests are surfaced immediately.

Most assistants deal with 80 to 150 emails daily. If you support multiple principals, that number can jump to 400. This volume creates a constant state of low-level anxiety. You are always wondering if you missed a message from a key stakeholder or a board member. The cognitive load of deciding what to do with each message is higher than the act of typing the reply itself.
Why email management feels like an uphill battle

The primary cause of email stress is the lack of a finish line. Email is an open loop. Unlike a document that you finish and save, an inbox is never truly empty. Every time you clear it, three more messages arrive. This creates a psychological effect where your brain never switches into deep work mode.

Another issue is context fragmentation. You are often jumping between Outlook, your calendar, and project management tools like Asana or Notion. This switching costs time. Research shows that context switching can decrease your productivity by up to 40 percent. Every time you leave your email to check a date on your calendar, you lose focus.
Fixes anyone can use for better email flow

items: Use the Four D method: Delete, Delegate, Defer, or Do. Apply this to every email you open.
Batch your inbox sessions. Check email at 9 AM, 1 PM, and 4 PM. Close the app in between.
Set up shared mailboxes. This allows you to work in an email account without needing the executive's password.
Create templates for common responses. If you send the same meeting invite or status update, do not type it from scratch.
Turn off all non-essential notifications. Only allow alerts for VIP senders like your principal or key clients.

blocks.text: How to use Lazur to manage your email load

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in your Mac notch. It sees your screen and helps you work faster. It does not click buttons for you, but it acts as a shortcut to get things done. When you are buried in email, you can hold the shortcut to ask Lazur to summarize a long thread or draft a reply.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask Lazur about any email on your screen. You can ask what the next step is for a meeting request or to find a specific date in a long thread.
blocks.title: Get context instantly

blocks.text: If you need to write a quick reply to a vendor, hold the fn key to dictate your response. Lazur cleans up your speech and types it into the cursor position. You can use your own snippets to save time on common phrases.

faq.question: How do executive assistants manage emails without burning out?
faq.answer: They use strict batching, clear delegation rules, and AI tools to handle the repetitive parts of drafting and research.

faq.question: Does Lazur read my emails?
faq.answer: Lazur only looks at your screen when you hold the shortcut key. It does not store your content or train models on your data.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur for sensitive client data?
faq.answer: If you work in a regulated field, always follow your company policy regarding data privacy and the use of AI tools.
